paragraphs.original: Today on The 10, we start with a major legal development that could change the landscape of social media. paragraphs.original: We begin in London with some uplifting health news that really is a breath of fresh air. paragraphs.cloze: We begin in London with some uplifting health news that really is a breath of fresh air. A new study suggests the British capital's efforts to cut [[Q01]] in recent years may be helping children's lungs grow healthier. Researchers focused on the city's ultra-low emission zone, introduced in central London in 2019.

paragraphs.original: Drivers of vehicles that don't meet strict emission standards have to pay a daily charge, the idea being to put the brakes on tailpipe pollution. The study tracked thousands of kids in London and nearby Luton over several years. Before the clean air zone began, London's kids had higher exposure to traffic pollution and lower average lung function.
paragraphs.cloze: Drivers of vehicles that don't meet strict [[Q02]] have to pay a daily charge, the idea being to put the brakes on tailpipe pollution. The study tracked thousands of kids in London and nearby Luton over several years. Before the clean air zone began, London's kids had higher exposure to traffic pollution and lower average lung function.

paragraphs.original: But over the four years, between 2018 and 2022, researchers observed a 5% drop in children with clinically impaired lung function in London. In Luton, which didn't have a clean air zone but did make other changes like adding bike paths and lowering speed limits, the rate fell 2%. Researchers say this is the first evidence that clean air zones may actually help child development.

paragraphs.original: That matters because lungs do most of their growing while we're young. If they don't fully develop by early adulthood, the risk rises later in life for conditions including asthma, emphysema, and chronic bronchitis. So, this isn't just about cleaner air today. paragraphs.original: As the U.S. will soon mark 25 years since the terrorist attack, retired United Airlines flight attendant Paul Pauli Veneto is pushing an airline beverage cart 220 miles from Boston to Ground Zero in New York City.
paragraphs.cloze: As the U.S. will soon mark 25 years since the terrorist attack, retired United Airlines [[Q28]] Paul Pauli Veneto is pushing an airline beverage cart 220 miles from Boston to Ground Zero in New York City.

paragraphs.original: The 67-year-old has previously traveled more than 750 miles since launching Pauli's Push in 2021, following routes symbolizing the flight paths of the four hijacked planes.
paragraphs.cloze: The 67-year-old has previously traveled more than 750 miles since launching Pauli's Push in 2021, following routes [[Q29]] the flight paths of the four hijacked planes.

paragraphs.original: I made a promise to myself that I would make sure these crew members of these aircrafts were honored and recognized for their heroics. So I went and got four more beverage carts, and I designed each one for each airplane.

paragraphs.original: Pauli adorned each cart with pictures of the crew members that were lost that day. His journey will take him across 60 cities and towns over a span of 28 days each step, honoring the lives lost on September 11th.
